sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Since the Torah is eternal, the command to make a Sanctuary and G-d's indwelling within it applies eternally in every generation, including during exile, and likewise all details of the Exodus and the Egyptian exile provide eternal instructions for every generation, including the current exile.

translations.translation: Now, since the Torah is eternal,
it is understood
that this matter
("And they shall make Me a Sanctuary and I will dwell in their midst")
is eternal throughout all generations,
even during the time of exile,
when because of our sins we were exiled from our land and distanced from our soil,
that even then there exist
(spiritually)
all the instructions and commandments
(of which it is written "and live by them")
that are dependent on the Mishkan and the Temple.
And so too is it regarding all the details that were in the Exodus from Egypt,
and even before that in the Egyptian exile,
that they are eternal instructions in every generation,
until this very day.
And as is known
regarding the matter of "and they embittered their lives with hard labor, in mortar and bricks, etc.",
that even now in the final exile there is the labor of mortar and bricks
(as it is in spirituality),
"mortar" refers to kal v'chomer (a fortiori reasoning) and "bricks" refers to libun hilchesa (clarification of halachah),
and through this they will subsequently merit the future redemption,
similar to the redemption of the Exodus from Egypt
(after the hard labor of mortar and bricks, etc.),
"and the children of Israel went out with an upraised hand."

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The greatness of engaging in Torah study during the time of exile is explained by the Baal HaHilula in the tenth section of the continuation of maamarim for the day of the Hilula, which describes how the Holy One, blessed be He, and the ministering angels listen to the voice of the Congregation of Israel studying Torah in synagogues and study halls even while scattered in exile.

translations.translation: Now, the greatness of engaging in Torah study during the time of exile
is explained by the Baal HaHilula in the tenth section
[the tenth shall be holy]
of the continuation of maamarim of the day of the Hilula,
which section is the conclusion and seal of the second maamar of the continuation,
beginning with the discourse "You who dwell in the gardens, companions listen to your voice, let Me hear it"
(according to Rashi's commentary on the verse),

"The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the Congregation of Israel, who are scattered in exile and shepherds in the gardens of others, etc., and nevertheless dwell in synagogues and study halls to engage in Torah,"
"the companions, who are the ministering angels
(and also the Holy One, blessed be He,
so to speak)
listen to your voice."

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The maamar continues that because of this, Israel are called the "hosts of Hashem," a name given specifically at the Exodus from Egypt, which relates to the sparks of holiness they refined during the Egyptian exile, and this connects to the theme of "You who dwell in the gardens" — through the Congregation of Israel's Torah study and mitzvah observance while scattered in exile, they refine the sparks of holiness in exile.

translations.translation: And the maamar continues,
that because of this Israel are called the "hosts of Hashem," as it is written,
"And it came to pass on that very day, all the hosts of Hashem went out of the land of Egypt."
For this name
("hosts of Hashem")
was given to Israel specifically at their Exodus from Egypt.
And one must explain the connection of the matters,
for that at the time of the Exodus from Egypt Israel were called "hosts of Hashem" is because of the sparks
(the hosts)
that were refined during the Egyptian exile
(as will be explained later).
And this is the connection of the matter of Israel being called "hosts of Hashem" to the subject of "You who dwell in the gardens,"

for through the service of the Congregation of Israel in their engagement with Torah and the fulfillment of its commandments while they are scattered in exile and shepherding in the gardens of others,
through this they refine the sparks that are in exile,
similar to "and they despoiled"
Egypt.
